clue.text: Grandma's questioned about dancing in disguise

indicators.note: one sense of 'about' is around or within, so the letters lie somewhere inside the neighbouring words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: An old woman is interrogated about something she got up to on the dance floor.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s of 'Grandma's' is part of the run, so ignore the punctuation and read straight through.
explanation.definitionFit: A masque was a courtly entertainment of music and dance in which performers wore masks and costume.

clue.text: Second gymnast works in rotation

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a very short time
Simone Biles, the American Olympic gymnast

explanation.surface: A gymnast who comes second turns in performances full of spins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Works' looks like a verb about the gymnast's routine; it is a noun, meaning works of art.
explanation.definitionFit: Mobiles are hanging sculptures whose suspended parts turn slowly in moving air, so they are artworks that rotate.

clue.text: Son given obligation by Crazy Horse?

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son
an IOU is a written promise to repay a debt
'by' as in multiplication, three by four, written with the times sign

explanation.surface: A son is landed with a debt by a mad horse.
explanation.walkthrough: Crazy Horse was a famous war leader of the Lakota people; the question mark shows he is an example of the answer rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Crazy Horse belonged to the Lakota, a people of the Great Plains grouped under that nation's name, so he exemplifies it.

clue.text: Set about tanker due for dismantling

indicators.note: something being dismantled is taken apart, so its letters can be rebuilt in another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Workers begin breaking up an old oil ship that is scheduled for scrapping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' belongs to the definition, not the wordplay: 'set about' is a phrasal verb meaning begin.
explanation.definitionFit: To set about a task and to undertake it both mean to begin it or commit oneself to doing it.

clue.text: Swapping East and West essentially across

indicators.note: a swap trades one thing for another, so one letter is taken out and a different one put in its place

parts.note: 'at heart' means essentially, fundamentally
compass abbreviation, the letter removed
compass abbreviation, the letter put in

explanation.surface: A note on exchanging the compass points, which are basically across from each other.
explanation.walkthrough: AT HEART with its E replaced by W becomes ATHWART. 'East and West' look like a pair to exchange with each other; really one replaces the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Athwart is an old and nautical word meaning from side to side, crosswise, transversely over something.

clue.text: Night in Paris stretching one's allowance

indicators.note: a word that is stretched has been pulled open, leaving room for something else inside it

parts.note: 'any one' and 'any' can stand for each other, as in 'take one' and 'take any'
the French word for night

explanation.surface: An evening in the French capital eats deep into someone's spending money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' standing for ANY is the leap here: 'pick one' and 'pick any' mean the same. 'In Paris' is a common way of asking for the French word.
explanation.definitionFit: An annuity is a fixed yearly sum paid to someone, an income or allowance that comes regularly.

clue.text: Lengthy drama shows heady invention?

indicators.note: to show something is to display it, and the letters are on display inside the words before

parts.note: the last two letters of the first word and the first three of the second

explanation.surface: A long play reveals a writer's dizzying creativity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heady' normally means intoxicating; here it means full of heads, which is why the definition carries a question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hydra was a mythical serpent with many heads that regrew when cut off, so it was a fabled creature of many heads.

clue.text: Tennis pros feel bitter about now

parts.note: the Association of Tennis Professionals, which runs the men's tour
to resent something is to feel bitter about it

explanation.surface: Professional tennis players are aggrieved by the current state of things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a container signal, but it belongs to the phrase 'feel bitter about', which is one verb.
explanation.definitionFit: At present is an idiom meaning at this moment, currently, in the time being.

clue.text: Old pub bores critically examine silverware

indicators.note: to bore is to drill a hole into something, so one part tunnels inside another

parts.note: to try a case in court is to examine it judicially
O is a standard abbreviation for old
PH, public house, as marked on British maps

explanation.surface: Tiresome regulars in an ancient tavern pore over the pots on the shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bores' looks like a noun for tedious people; it is the verb, drilling into TRY.
explanation.definitionFit: In sport, silverware is slang for cups and other prizes, the trophies a team wins.

clue.text: Japanese finalist in karaoke butchered Rolling Stones?

parts.note: J is the abbreviation for Japanese

indicators.note: the finalist is whoever is left at the end, so only the closing letter is taken

parts.note: the final letter of the word

indicators.note: something rolling turns over, so the letters come round the other way

parts.note: slew is the past tense of slay, to kill

explanation.surface: A Japanese singer in the karaoke final murdered a Rolling Stones song.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface welds 'Rolling Stones' into the band's name; split it, and 'Rolling' works on the slaughter word while 'Stones' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Precious gems are commonly called stones, as in a ring set with three stones, so they are jewels.

clue.text: Baron abed with beating pulse

indicators.note: a beating batters something out of shape, so the letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A nobleman lies in bed with his heart racing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' and 'beating' together suggest a heartbeat; 'pulse' is the food sense, an edible seed.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulses are the edible seeds of legumes such as peas, lentils and beans, and the broad bean is one.

clue.text: Drop very much required by this drinker

parts.note: a dip is a fall, as in a dip in prices
as in 'I love it so'

explanation.surface: A heavy drinker can never get enough of one more drop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop' reads as a drop of drink; in the wordplay it is a fall or dip.
explanation.definitionFit: Dipso is informal shortening of dipsomaniac, a person with an uncontrollable craving for alcohol.

clue.text: City of temples left by Roman wife

parts.note: L is the standard abbreviation for left
uxor is the Latin word for wife

explanation.surface: A Roman man's wife walks out and leaves him in a city of shrines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roman' signals a Latin word, as 'in Paris' signals French.
explanation.definitionFit: Luxor in Egypt stands on the site of ancient Thebes and is famous for the Karnak and Luxor temple complexes.

clue.text: Queen bee hit fifty travelling around South Africa

indicators.note: to be around something is to surround it, so one part encloses another
things that travel move about, so the letters are moved into another order

parts.note: taken as written
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
ZA is the international code for South Africa

explanation.surface: A queen bee makes a half-century while touring South Africa, as if bees played cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen bee' reads as one insect; split it, and 'Queen' is the definition. ZA comes from Zuid-Afrika, the Dutch name.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth is the name of two English queens, most recently Elizabeth II, so it stands for a queen.

clue.text: Greek city state's regressive governors

indicators.note: to regress is to go backwards, so the letters run from the end to the start

parts.note: Sparta was the warlike city state of ancient Greece, with the possessive s

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek polis is said to have rulers who turned back the clock.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive s on 'state's' is kept as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Satraps were the provincial governors of the ancient Persian empire, and by extension any petty local rulers.

clue.text: Quantity of leaf cut up in brew

indicators.note: a brew is a concoction stirred together, so the letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Instructions for how much chopped tea leaf goes into a pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut up' looks like the anagram signal, but its letters are needed in the fodder; 'brew' does the stirring.
explanation.definitionFit: A teacupful is a measure of amount, as much as one teacup holds, used in old recipes.

clue.text: Clodhopper changing hands to catch right ball

indicators.note: to catch something is to hold it, so one part is held inside another
switching from one hand to the other trades a side for its opposite, so one letter is exchanged for another

parts.note: a yokel is a clumsy country bumpkin
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A clumsy fielder switches hands to hold a catch.
explanation.walkthrough: YOKEL turns its L (left) into R (right) to give YOKER, which then takes in another R. A yorker is a cricket delivery pitched right at the batter's feet.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a yorker is a kind of delivery bowled to land at the batsman's toes, so it is a ball.

clue.text: Once again, appropriate range limited sound of singers

indicators.note: something limited is cut short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: reach, the extent of range, with its last letter cut

indicators.note: the sound of something is what is heard, so a spoken word is spelt differently

parts.note: a group of singers, spelt in the old way

explanation.surface: A choir with a narrow vocal range is put to good use again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' is a verb here, to take possession of. Quire is an old spelling of choir and also a set of sheets of paper.
explanation.definitionFit: To reacquire is to obtain or take possession of again, and to appropriate is to take something for oneself.

clue.text: Having bowled, look round pavilion

parts.note: to gaze is to look steadily
b is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for bowled
the letter O is round

explanation.surface: A cricketer finishes bowling an over and glances around the clubhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket setting makes 'pavilion' the clubhouse; the answer is a garden pavilion.
explanation.definitionFit: A gazebo is a small open-sided garden summerhouse, a pavilion with a view.

clue.text: To show off more in public, dress up

parts.note: out in the open, publicly known

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means reading from bottom to top, the opposite way

parts.note: garb is clothing, dress

explanation.surface: Someone advises getting dolled up in order to make a bigger display in front of others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dress up' reads as a phrasal verb; the 'up' is the turnaround signal for the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To outbrag someone is to boast more than they do, to beat them at showing off.

clue.text: Old performer literally discharged dead

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
an act is a performer or group on a bill

indicators.note: to discharge is to unload, so the word's contents go and only its shell remains

parts.note: just the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: An aged actor was let go from the company and has quite literally died.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead' sounds like the end of the story; it is an adverb, as in dead right or dead centre.
explanation.definitionFit: Dead as an adverb means precisely or absolutely, as in dead on time, so it means exactly.

clue.text: See new TV game shows

indicators.note: a game leg is a lame or crooked one, so the letters are out of shape

parts.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new
taken as written

explanation.surface: An invitation to catch the latest quiz programmes on television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game shows' reads as one television phrase; split it, and 'game' is the signal while 'shows' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Events such as horse shows, galas and exhibitions are public occasions or spectacles, which is what shows are.

clue.text: Surrendered, caught starting with other side in folly

indicators.note: starting with something new means the opening letter is exchanged for it

parts.note: a fielder who has fielded the ball has caught or stopped it

indicators.note: of a word's two sides, its start and its finish, the other one is the end

parts.note: the closing letter of the word, opposite its F

explanation.surface: Someone gave in, trapped in an act of foolishness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Folly' begins with F, like FIELDED; swapping in its other end, Y, gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To yield is to give way or concede, so having yielded means having given in to an opponent.

clue.text: Part of neck, namely collar

parts.note: sc, scilicet, Latin for namely
a ruff is a stiff frilled collar of Elizabethan dress

explanation.surface: Pointing out which part of the neck a collar sits on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collar' also suggests grabbing someone, which is what you do by the answer; but here it is the frilled neckwear.
explanation.definitionFit: The scruff is the back of the neck, the nape, especially where a cat or person is grabbed.

clue.text: Pained expression on entering this French carriage

indicators.note: to enter something is to go inside it, so one part sits within another

parts.note: cette is the French feminine for this
a cry of pain

explanation.surface: Someone winces as they climb into a train compartment in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This French' asks for the French word for this.
explanation.definitionFit: A couchette is a railway carriage with fold-down berths for sleeping, used on European night trains.

clue.text: Pilgrim in holy war had moved to the top

indicators.note: in a down clue the top is the start, so a closing chunk is shifted round to the front

parts.note: a jihad is a holy war

explanation.surface: A pilgrim caught up in a crusade has had to climb to the summit.
explanation.walkthrough: The signal names the chunk that travels: the last three letters of the holy war, which spell 'had', go to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A hadji is a Muslim who has made the hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, and the word is used as a title of respect.

clue.text: Waiters should be prompt when this is delivered

indicators.note: a line or speech that is delivered is spoken out, so the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: a cue is the prompt that tells an actor to speak

explanation.surface: Restaurant staff ought to be quick once a dish has been served.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waiters' are not table staff but people waiting their turn, and 'prompt' is not an adjective meaning quick but a noun, the theatrical prompt.
explanation.definitionFit: A line of people standing and waiting their turn is made up of waiters in the literal sense of the word.

clue.text: Last words from Victor, rude shout after nurse

parts.note: EN, Enrolled Nurse
Victor is V in the radio alphabet
'oi!' is a rude call for attention

explanation.surface: A dying man named Victor rudely shouts at the nurse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After nurse' puts EN first. 'Oi' is the British cry of 'hey, you!'.
explanation.definitionFit: An envoi is the short closing stanza of a poem or the concluding remarks of a book, its parting words.

clue.text: Hungry bunny linked to field being regularly plundered

indicators.note: plundering at regular intervals strips out every other letter, leaving the rest

parts.note: the second and fourth letters
the first, third and fifth letters, continuing the same alternation

explanation.surface: A starving rabbit raids a nearby field.
explanation.walkthrough: Run the two words together as one string and keep every second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unfed has not been given food, so they are hungry.

clue.text: Driver, with tee shot, recovered

indicators.note: something shot is ruined or wrecked, so the letters are broken up and reordered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A golfer uses a driver for the tee shot and gets the ball back in play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driver' and 'tee shot' set up golf; 'shot' is the signal, not part of the stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: To retrieve something is to get it back, which is to recover it.

clue.text: River fish in decline

parts.note: the Fal is a river in Cornwall
the ling is a long sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: Fish stocks in a river are dwindling.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fal is a short river in Cornwall, south-west England, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Something falling is dropping or diminishing, which is what being in decline means.

clue.text: Tear-covered note to serve as memento

indicators.note: something covered has a layer over it, so one part is wrapped around another

parts.note: to rend is to tear
mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A tear-stained letter is kept as a keepsake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear' reads as a teardrop; it is the verb that rhymes with bear, meaning rip.
explanation.definitionFit: A memento prompts memory of someone or something, which is what it does when it helps people recall the past.
